rv.q: Happily, the rest of the cast rises to the challenge, and “Lend Me a Tenor” is exactly what it needs to be: hilarious.
You have to be a little nuts to do justice to farce, with its maniacal fixations and blinding panics and fears.
For it's a good-hearted show with real laughs: not to be sniffed at.
Tucci's ensemble nails just about every hyper-physical take in the comedy archives, building to the recap that telescopes all the action into about 45 seconds of sweet dazzle.

The timid prompter, Max, must put on Tito's tights to save the evening and get his girl. Peter Sham and Brad Carroll's show tries to refurbish stale material. (It's based on Ken Ludwig's 1986 comedy.) Despite the nitwit plot, Ian Talbot's production just about wins you over, with vitality, florid-fancy sets and an old-fashioned appeal.
Not terrible, not terrific, then - something best left to the tourists maybe?

In all the harum-scarum high jinks of “Lend Me a Tenor,” Ken Ludwig’s romp about opera (slickly directed by Stanley Tucci, at the Music Box), there is a lot of theatrical panache on display, but not one idea.

But the heady ether of prime farce never materializes in this labor-intensive but laugh-deficient evening, directed by Stanley Tucci and starring Tony Shalhoub as the desperate impresario and Anthony LaPaglia as the troublesome tenor.
It's a genius move, a perfectly enchanting button to an already solid, mirthful show.
This time around, the unhilarity is almost uninterrupted, and sometimes magnified by miscasting and flaccid pacing.
Ken Ludwig's 1989 play is an imperfect farce — a bit slow, too long and without a properly wild conclusion.

Ken Ludwig’s quarter-century old “Lend Me a Tenor” is revived on Broadway with a deft cast including Tony Shalhoub, Anthony LaPaglia and Jan Maxwell, under the direction of that expert comedian Stanley Tucci. And as before, it entertains.
When I read “Lend Me a Tenor,” it was perfect: hilarious, well written and so intricately plotted.
Thankfully, one subpar performance doesn't flatten Tenor's high notes, or deflate its giddy spirit.
The original production was a major hit and a similar success looks likely for this brightly performed and highly enjoyable Broadway revival which opened Sunday at the Theatre.
Perfecting the comic timing and broad style required to stage the play is no easy task, and it shows that Tucci may have a future as a director ahead.

cn.t: This crowd-pleasing farce revival earns mostly positive reviews for its expert ensemble cast and high-energy slapstick, though some critics dismiss the material as mindless and lacking substance beneath all the door-slamming chaos.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.
